Compiling the complete picture now.\n\n---\n\n## CF Workers: Sustained 1-Hour Execution — Documented Patterns\n\n### The Core Problem\n\nCF Workers are fire-and-die by design. A standard `fetch()` handler has a **30-second wall-time hard limit**. `ctx.waitUntil()` does NOT extend this — it only allows cleanup after response transmission. Self-invoking via `fetch()` within the same worker does not reset the clock. This cannot be worked around within the standard Workers model.\n\nThere are four legitimate patterns. Here they are ranked by fitness for a 1-hour continuous queue processor.\n\n---\n\n### Pattern 1: Cloudflare Workflows (BEST FIT for 1-hour queue processing)\n\n**Source:** [Cloudflare Workflows GA announcement](https://blog.cloudflare.com/workflows-ga-production-ready-durable-execution/) | [Workflows limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/reference/limits/)\n\n**How it works:** Step-based durable execution engine built on Workers. Each `step.do()` call is independently retriable with state automatically persisted between steps. CPU is billed only for active execution; wall time between steps costs nothing.\n\n**Hard limits (Paid plan):**\n- Max steps per workflow: 10,000 (configurable to 25,000)\n- Max sleep per `step.sleep`: 365 days\n- Sleep steps do NOT count toward the 10,000-step limit\n- CPU per step: 30 seconds default, configurable to 5 minutes\n- Wall time per step: unlimited\n- Overall workflow duration: theoretically unlimited across steps\n- Concurrent running instances: 50,000 (Paid); waiting/sleeping instances are free and excluded from this count\n- Max persisted state: 1 GB (Paid)\n\n**Pattern for 1-hour continuous queue:**\n```javascript\nexport class QueueWorkflow extends WorkflowEntrypoint {\n  async run(event, step) {\n    while (true) {\n      const batch = await step.do('fetch-batch', async () =&gt; {\n        return await fetchNextQueueBatch(); // 30s CPU budget per step\n      });\n      if (batch.length === 0) {\n        await step.sleep('idle-wait', '30 seconds');\n        continue;\n      }\n      for (const item of batch) {\n        await step.do(`process-${item.id}`, async () =&gt; {\n          return await processItem(item);\n        });\n      }\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nEach `step.do` gets a fresh 30-second CPU budget and is independently retriable. The workflow persists across reboots, evictions, and deploys.\n\n**Verdict:** Correct architecture for a 1-hour queue processor. You are not running one continuous 1-hour invocation — you are running a durable state machine that processes chunks indefinitely.\n\n---\n\n### Pattern 2: Durable Objects + Alarms (GOOD — stateful, but more manual)\n\n**Source:** [DO Alarms docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/alarms/) | [DO limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/platform/limits/)\n\n**How it works:** A Durable Object sets a recurring alarm against itself. Each alarm invocation gets 15 minutes of wall time. The alarm reschedules itself before completing, creating a self-sustaining heartbeat.\n\n**Hard limits:**\n- CPU per invocation: 30 seconds default, 5 minutes configurable\n- Wall time per alarm invocation: **15 minutes hard cap**\n- Retry on failure: at-least-once, exponential backoff, up to 6 retries\n- Alarm schedule precision: minimum 1 second granularity\n\n**Pattern:**\n```javascript\nclass QueueProcessor {\n  async alarm() {\n    // Each alarm gets 15 min wall time\n    const batch = await this.fetchBatch();\n    await this.processBatch(batch);\n    // Reschedule itself to keep running\n    await this.state.storage.setAlarm(Date.now() + 100); // 100ms gap\n  }\n}\n```\n\n**Gap:** 15-minute alarm cap means you cannot run one continuous invocation for an hour. You chain alarm → alarm → alarm. State must be persisted to DO SQLite between invocations. Gaps between alarms are possible (Cloudflare fires alarms \"within a minute of the scheduled time\" not exactly). For queue processing this is fine — items sit in queue until next alarm fires.\n\n**Verdict:** Works for 1-hour operation via chained 15-minute invocations. More complex than Workflows — you own all state management. Better if you need tight stateful control (e.g., in-memory position tracking that you SQLite-persist yourself).\n\n---\n\n### Pattern 3: Cloudflare Queues + Consumer Worker (GOOD — for pure throughput)\n\n**Source:** [How Queues works](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/reference/how-queues-works/) | [DEV.to long jobs post](https://dev.to/teaganga/triggering-long-jobs-in-cloudflare-workers-8mh)\n\n**How it works:** The queue consumer handler (`queue()`) has **no CPU time limit** — only a wall-time limit measured in minutes (not seconds). Cloudflare auto-scales concurrent consumers to drain the queue. Messages not acknowledged get redelivered.\n\n**Hard limits (from official docs and dev.to article):**\n- CPU time: unlimited in queue consumer\n- Wall time: minutes (exact ceiling not documented; community reports 15 min per batch)\n- Max message size: 128 KB\n- Max batch size: 100 messages\n- Consumer concurrency: auto-scaled by CF based on queue depth and failure rate\n- At-least-once delivery; explicit ack/nack per message\n\n**Pattern:**\n```javascript\nexport default {\n  async queue(batch, env, ctx) {\n    for (const message of batch.messages) {\n      await processItem(message.body);\n      message.ack(); // Or nack() to redeliver\n    }\n    // CF delivers next batch automatically\n  }\n}\n```\n\n**Key distinction from Workflows:** Queues are pull-based with CF-controlled delivery. You don't control the \"loop\" — CF does. If you need to sustain processing for 1 hour, you need items in the queue for 1 hour. The consumer runs continuously as long as items exist.\n\n**Verdict:** Best for high-throughput processing where tasks are discrete and queue-resident. Not suitable if you need a single \"session\" that tracks shared state across 1 hour — each batch invocation is stateless.\n\n---\n\n### Pattern 4: Durable Objects + `keepAlive()` / Long-Polling WebSocket (NICHE)\n\n**Source:** [CF Agents long-running docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/concepts/long-running-agents/)\n\n**How it works:** A persistent WebSocket connection to a DO resets the CPU timer to 30 seconds on each incoming message. The DO is never evicted while the connection is open. Wall time is unlimited while connected.\n\n**Hard limits:**\n- CPU per WebSocket message: 30 seconds (resets each message)\n- Wall time: unlimited while connection is open\n- Connection must remain open — if client disconnects, eviction can occur\n\n**Pattern:**\n```typescript\nconst result = await this.keepAliveWhile(async () =&gt; {\n  // Heartbeats prevent eviction; CPU resets each heartbeat message\n  return await runLongOperation();\n});\n```\n\n**Verdict:** Designed for interactive agents (human-in-loop). Not appropriate for unattended 1-hour queue processing — requires an always-open network connection to prevent eviction.\n\n---\n\n### Hard Limit Summary Table\n\n| Pattern | CPU Per Invocation | Wall Time Per Invocation | 1-Hour Sustained? | State Persistence |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Standard `fetch()` | 30s (free) / configurable | **30s hard** | No | None |\n| `ctx.waitUntil()` | Same as fetch | Same as fetch | No | None |\n| Cron trigger + scheduled() | 30s (free) / configurable | Unlimited (Paid) | No (fires once/interval) | None (use KV/DO manually) |\n| Queue consumer | **Unlimited CPU** | Minutes | Yes (continuous) | None per invocation |\n| DO alarm chain | 5 min (configurable) | **15 min per alarm** | Yes (chained) | DO SQLite |\n| DO + WebSocket | 30s/message | Unlimited (connected) | Yes (if connected) | DO SQLite |\n| Workflows | 5 min/step | **Unlimited per step** | **Yes (best fit)** | 1 GB engine-managed |\n\n---\n\n### Verdict: Best Practice for 1-Hour Sustained Queue Processing\n\n**Cloudflare Workflows is the documented best-practice architecture.** It is the only pattern where:\n1. The 1-hour operation is a first-class durable construct (not a workaround)\n2. State survives crashes, deploys, and evictions automatically\n3. Each processing unit (step) gets independent retry with no shared failure blast radius\n4. Wall time is unlimited; you pay only for active CPU\n5. Concurrent scale is 50,000 instances (Paid)\n\n**Durable Objects + Alarms is the correct fallback** if you need fine-grained stateful control that Workflows does not provide — but you own all checkpoint/recovery logic.\n\n**Queues alone** works if the problem is purely throughput-shaped (discrete tasks, stateless per batch). Does not support a single coordinated 1-hour \"session.\"\n\n**Any pattern that tries to run one Worker invocation continuously for 1 hour will fail** — the platform is designed against this. The correct mental model is: a durable identity (Workflow or DO) that wakes, processes a chunk, persists state, and sleeps — cycling for as long as needed.\n\nSources:\n- [Long-Running Agents — Cloudflare Agents docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/concepts/long-running-agents/)\n- [Cloudflare Workflows Limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/reference/limits/)\n- [Workflows GA — production-ready durable execution](https://blog.cloudflare.com/workflows-ga-production-ready-durable-execution/)\n- [Durable Objects Limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/platform/limits/)\n- [Durable Objects Alarms](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/alarms/)\n- [How Cloudflare Queues Works](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/reference/how-queues-works/)\n- [Triggering Long Jobs in Cloudflare Workers — DEV Community](https://dev.to/teaganga/triggering-long-jobs-in-cloudflare-workers-8mh)\n- [CF Workers Limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/)\n- [Higher CPU Limits — CF Changelog 2025-03-25](https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2025-03-25-higher-cpu-limits/)</result>\n<usage><subagent_tokens>35173</subagent_tokens><tool_uses>11</tool_uses><duration_ms>117678</duration_ms></usage>\n</task-notification>"}

Here is the full research report.\n\n---\n\n## Research Report: Serverless Worker Competition Frameworks &amp; Agent Scoring Methodology\n\n---\n\n### 1. Does a \"serverless worker competition\" framework exist?\n\n**Short answer: No exact match exists.** Nothing in the literature describes multiple CF Workers or Lambda functions racing each other competitively on a shared task pool, scored in real time by throughput + discovery rate. What exists splits into two disconnected bodies:\n\n- **Serverless performance benchmarks** — compare providers (CF vs Lambda vs GCF) on latency, cold start, and cost. No competitive/racing element. No scoring against peers.\n- **AI agent evaluation benchmarks** — score agent task completion quality and throughput, but against a fixed task corpus, not against competing peer workers.\n\nThe intersection — autonomous worker competition with live scoring — does not yet exist as a published framework.\n\n---\n\n### 2. Serverless Benchmarking: What Exists\n\n**SeBS (Serverless Benchmark Suite)** — ETH Zurich, Middleware '21, updated 2025\n- URL: [github.com/spcl/serverless-benchmarks](https://github.com/spcl/serverless-benchmarks)\n- Tests AWS Lambda, GCF, Azure, and open-source platforms\n- Metrics: **function latency, throughput (invocations/sec), cold-start overhead, container eviction probability, billing time vs wall time, memory consumption**\n- Uses PAPI for low-level CPU counters; HTTP timing stripped of connection overhead via cURL\n- Does NOT score workers against each other — it scores the same function across providers\n\n**SeBS-Flow** (EuroSys '25 extension)\n- URL: [arxiv.org/pdf/2410.03480](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.03480)\n- Extends SeBS to multi-function workflow orchestration\n- Still provider-comparison, not inter-worker competition\n\n**serverless-benchmark.com** — continuous independent benchmark of Lambda / GCF / Azure / CF Workers\n- URL: [serverless-benchmark.com](https://serverless-benchmark.com/)\n- Tracks cold-start p50/p95, execution time, cost per million invocations\n- CF Workers benchmark result: **p95 = 242ms vs Lambda@Edge 842ms vs Lambda 1346ms** (Cloudflare's own data)\n\n**Cloudflare's own methodology:**\n- Uses Catchpoint for global network-distributed timing\n- Measures TCP connect, TTFB, TTLB at p50/p95/mean\n- Result: Workers 30% faster than 3 years ago at P90, 210% faster than Lambda@Edge\n- URL: [blog.cloudflare.com/unpacking-cloudflare-workers-cpu-performance-benchmarks](https://blog.cloudflare.com/unpacking-cloudflare-workers-cpu-performance-benchmarks/)\n\n**Key gap:** None of these frameworks pit workers against each other. They all benchmark the same function against external baselines, not peer workers competing for task credit.\n\n---\n\n### 3. AI Agent Evaluation: What Exists\n\n#### HAL — Holistic Agent Leaderboard (Princeton)\n- URL: [hal.cs.princeton.edu](https://hal.cs.princeton.edu/)\n- Paper: [arxiv.org/pdf/2510.11977](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.11977)\n- **Best existing methodology for multi-dimensional agent scoring**\n- Validated via 21,730 agent rollouts, 9 models, 9 benchmarks, ~$40k compute\n- Metrics tracked:\n  - Accuracy / task success rate\n  - **Cost** (dollars spent per task solved — Pareto frontier of score vs. cost)\n  - **Reliability** (variance across runs, abstention rate, robustness to adversarial inputs)\n  - Error frequency (AgentError vs EnvironmentError distinguished)\n  - Shortcuts detected via LLM log auditor (Docent)\n- Automatically computes Pareto frontier: \"given $X budget, which agent wins?\"\n- Does not score agents competing for the same task pool simultaneously — each agent runs independently against a fixed corpus\n\n#### TheAgentCompany Benchmark\n- URL: [arxiv.org/abs/2412.14161](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14161)\n- 175 enterprise tasks in a simulated software company environment\n- **Scoring formula:**\n  - `S_full` = 1 if all checkpoints passed, 0 otherwise\n  - `S_partial` = weighted sum of checkpoint fractions (partial credit)\n  - Deterministic evaluators (Python state checks) + LLM judges for free-form outputs\n  - Tasks have intermediate milestones worth fractional credit — not all-or-nothing\n- Current top: Gemini-2.5-Pro 30.3% full / 39.3% partial; Claude-3.7-Sonnet 26.3% / 36.4%\n\n#### MASEval (March 2026)\n- URL: [arxiv.org/abs/2603.08835](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.08835) | [maseval.readthedocs.io](https://maseval.readthedocs.io/en/stable/)\n- Universal adapter layer: any agent system, any benchmark — \"pytest for multi-agent eval\"\n- Reports: Task Completion Rate, scaled Task Scores, structured error attribution\n- Explicitly separates AgentError (counts against score) from EnvironmentError (excludable)\n- Does not inherently support competitive/simultaneous worker racing — runs are independent\n\n#### GAIA Benchmark\n- 450 questions across 3 difficulty levels\n- Scoring: Pass@1 success rate; LLM-as-judge compares agent answer to ground truth\n- GAIA2 extension: Pareto frontier of accuracy vs. monetary cost\n- No competitive inter-agent element\n\n#### tau-bench (Sierra)\n- URL: [sierra.ai/blog/t-bench-leaderboard](https://sierra.ai/blog/t-bench-leaderboard)\n- Retail/airline multi-turn dialogue tasks\n- Metrics: pass@k (at least one success in k runs), pass^k (all k runs succeed)\n- Good for measuring consistency of agents under repeated runs\n\n---\n\n### 4. Best Scoring Methodology for Autonomous Worker Competition\n\nBased on what exists, here is the cleanest synthesis for scoring workers competing in a fixed time window:\n\n#### Primary Metrics (from the literature)\n\n| Metric | Source | Formula |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Task completion rate** | TheAgentCompany, GAIA | Tasks fully completed / Total tasks available |\n| **Partial credit score** | TheAgentCompany | Sum of checkpoint fractions (e.g., 3/5 checkpoints = 0.6) |\n| **Throughput** | SeBS, Wandb | Verified completions per second during window |\n| **Cost efficiency** | HAL, GAIA2 | Score / dollar spent (Pareto metric) |\n| **Discovery rate** | (novel — not in literature) | Unique items/threads found / Total available |\n| **Error-adjusted score** | MASEval | Raw score minus AgentError penalty |\n| **Consistency** | tau-bench | pass^k — how many runs the agent wins on ALL k trials |\n\n#### Recommended Composite Formula (synthesized from HAL + TheAgentCompany)\n\n```\nScore(W) = (α × TasksCompleted/TasksAvailable)\n         + (β × PartialCheckpointSum/MaxCheckpoints)\n         + (γ × UniqueItemsFound/TotalItems)\n         + (δ × ThreadsDiscovered/TotalThreads)\n         − (ε × ErrorRate)\n         − (ζ × CostSpent/CostBudget)\n```\n\nWhere α + β + γ + δ = 1.0 and ε, ζ are penalty coefficients.\n\n**Key insight from HAL:** The real differentiator is the **Pareto frontier** — not \"who scored highest\" but \"who scored highest per dollar spent.\" Workers that brute-force with high cost rank below efficient workers at the same accuracy tier.\n\n**Key insight from TheAgentCompany:** Partial credit prevents cliff-edge scoring. A worker that completes 3 of 5 checkpoints on 10 tasks should outscore a worker that completes 5 of 5 checkpoints on 4 tasks but abandons the rest.\n\n#### Fixed Time Window Design\n\nThe literature does not cover this directly, but the W&amp;B article on evaluating autonomous agents flags the anti-pattern: **raw throughput is misleading if agents sacrifice quality for volume.** The cited fix is the weighted formula `(Accurate completions × Complexity weight) / Time invested` — which prevents workers from gaming the competition by picking easy tasks.\n\nWeights by complexity class (task difficulty buckets) are the standard correction from benchmarks like GAIA's 3-level difficulty system.\n\n---\n\n### 5. Nearest Things to \"Agent Olympics\"\n\n- **HAL Reliability Dashboard** — [hal.cs.princeton.edu/reliability](https://hal.cs.princeton.edu/reliability/) — closest to a live competitive leaderboard across agents on the same benchmarks, with cost normalization\n- **Steel.dev Agent Leaderboard** — [leaderboard.steel.dev](https://leaderboard.steel.dev/) — browser/coding/computer-use agents ranked\n- **Galileo Agent Leaderboard** — [huggingface.co/spaces/galileo-ai/agent-leaderboard](https://huggingface.co/spaces/galileo-ai/agent-leaderboard) — 5 enterprise industry scenarios, multi-turn\n- **SWE-bench** — [swebench.com](https://www.swebench.com/) — coding agents racing on GitHub issues (closest to \"workers competing on task corpus\")\n- **ARC-AGI-3** (March 2026) — all frontier systems below 1% — too hard to differentiate current systems\n\nNone of these are real-time serverless worker races. Spins up multiple serverless workers (CF Workers, Lambda, etc.) simultaneously\n2. Points them at a shared live task pool\n3. Awards tasks claimed (dequeuing mechanics)\n4. Scores in real time on tasks completed + items discovered + threads found\n5. Normalizes by time window AND cost\n\nThis is a genuine gap. Each `step.do()` call is independently retriable with state automatically persisted between steps. CPU is billed only for active execution; wall time between steps costs nothing.\n\n**Hard limits (Paid plan):**\n- Max steps per workflow: 10,000 (configurable to 25,000)\n- Max sleep per `step.sleep`: 365 days\n- Sleep steps do NOT count toward the 10,000-step limit\n- CPU per step: 30 seconds default, configurable to 5 minutes\n- Wall time per step: unlimited\n- Overall workflow duration: theoretically unlimited across steps\n- Concurrent running instances: 50,000 (Paid); waiting/sleeping instances are free and excluded from this count\n- Max persisted state: 1 GB (Paid)\n\n**Pattern for 1-hour continuous queue:**\n```javascript\nexport class QueueWorkflow extends WorkflowEntrypoint {\n  async run(event, step) {\n    while (true) {\n      const batch = await step.do('fetch-batch', async () =&gt; {\n        return await fetchNextQueueBatch(); // 30s CPU budget per step\n      });\n      if (batch.length === 0) {\n        await step.sleep('idle-wait', '30 seconds');\n        continue;\n      }\n      for (const item of batch) {\n        await step.do(`process-${item.id}`, async () =&gt; {\n          return await processItem(item);\n        });\n      }\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nEach `step.do` gets a fresh 30-second CPU budget and is independently retriable. The workflow persists across reboots, evictions, and deploys.\n\n**Verdict:** Correct architecture for a 1-hour queue processor. You chain alarm → alarm → alarm. State must be persisted to DO SQLite between invocations. Gaps between alarms are possible (Cloudflare fires alarms \"within a minute of the scheduled time\" not exactly). For queue processing this is fine — items sit in queue until next alarm fires.\n\n**Verdict:** Works for 1-hour operation via chained 15-minute invocations. Cloudflare auto-scales concurrent consumers to drain the queue. Messages not acknowledged get redelivered.\n\n**Hard limits (from official docs and dev.to article):**\n- CPU time: unlimited in queue consumer\n- Wall time: minutes (exact ceiling not documented; community reports 15 min per batch)\n- Max message size: 128 KB\n- Max batch size: 100 messages\n- Consumer concurrency: auto-scaled by CF based on queue depth and failure rate\n- At-least-once delivery; explicit ack/nack per message\n\n**Pattern:**\n```javascript\nexport default {\n  async queue(batch, env, ctx) {\n    for (const message of batch.messages) {\n      await processItem(message.body);\n      message.ack(); // Or nack() to redeliver\n    }\n    // CF delivers next batch automatically\n  }\n}\n```\n\n**Key distinction from Workflows:** Queues are pull-based with CF-controlled delivery. You don't control the \"loop\" — CF does. If you need to sustain processing for 1 hour, you need items in the queue for 1 hour. The consumer runs continuously as long as items exist.\n\n**Verdict:** Best for high-throughput processing where tasks are discrete and queue-resident. Not suitable if you need a single \"session\" that tracks shared state across 1 hour — each batch invocation is stateless.\n\n---\n\n### Pattern 4: Durable Objects + `keepAlive()` / Long-Polling WebSocket (NICHE)\n\n**Source:** [CF Agents long-running docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/concepts/long-running-agents/)\n\n**How it works:** A persistent WebSocket connection to a DO resets the CPU timer to 30 seconds on each incoming message. Compiling the research report.\n\n---\n\n# PCC-3 Research Report: Autonomous Agent Loop Patterns for Fixed Time Windows\n\n## WHAT WAS ASKED\n\nBest practices for running an AI agent autonomously for 1 hour that: drains a backlog queue, logs discoveries, self-reports metrics, and competes against sibling agents.\n\n---\n\n## PATTERN 1 — The Planner-Worker-Judge Triad (Most Proven)\n\n**Source:** [nibzard/awesome-agentic-patterns](https://github.com/nibzard/awesome-agentic-patterns/blob/main/patterns/planner-worker-separation-for-long-running-agents.md)\n\nThe single most battle-tested pattern for long-running autonomous work. Three roles:\n\n- **Planner** — explores the queue/codebase, spawns sub-planners, creates tasks. Planning itself is parallelized and recursive.\n- **Worker** — operates in isolation, no cross-worker coordination. Executes only its assigned task.\n- **Judge** — evaluates whether objective is met or iteration should continue.\n\n**Key mechanic:** \"Fresh starts\" at each cycle. Workers get a new context window per task to prevent drift and tunnel vision. This is the anti-pattern to long-context degradation.\n\n**Proven scale:** Hundreds of concurrent workers running for weeks on large codebases.\n\n**Failure modes (documented):**\n- Over-coordination: an \"integrator\" quality-control role created more bottlenecks than it solved — eliminated in production.\n- Early termination: models \"tend to stop early and take shortcuts\" — Judge layer is the mitigation.\n- Context drift: agents lose goal fidelity over long runs without fresh-start cycles.\n\n---\n\n## PATTERN 2 — LangGraph StateGraph with Hard Budget Caps\n\n**Source:** [MatterAI self-correcting loops guide](https://www.matterai.so/guides/agentic-workflows-building-self-correcting-loops-with-langgraph-and-crewai-state-machines), [LangGraph timeout docs](https://langchain-cn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/modules/agents/agent_executors/examples/max_time_limit.html)\n\nLangGraph implements time-bounded execution via `should_continue()` gates on conditional edges. The `AgentState` TypedDict tracks:\n\n- `iterations` — retry count hard cap (5–15 iterations recommended)\n- `total_tokens` — cumulative spend (50k token ceiling common)\n- `quality_score` — normalized LLM-as-judge score (0–1)\n- `errors` — classified failure modes (syntax / logic / timeout / API)\n\n**For a 1-hour time window:** LangGraph does NOT enforce wall-clock deadlines natively. You inject `start_time = time.time()` into the state at initialization, and `should_continue()` checks `time.time() - start_time &lt; 3600`. No built-in scheduler. Entirely custom.\n\n**Durable execution (LangGraph v1.0+):** Compile graph with PostgreSQL checkpointer — `StateSnapshot` saved at every super-step keyed by `thread_id`. If the runner dies mid-session, `resume_from_checkpoint(thread_id)` picks up exactly where it stopped. Validated in production.\n\n**Failure modes:**\n- No clock enforcement without custom implementation — easy to miss.\n- Checkpointer adds latency per step — 50–200ms per DB write at scale.\n- `max_iterations=15` without wall-clock guard allows runaway if LLM calls are fast.\n\n---\n\n## PATTERN 3 — Cloudflare Durable Objects: Hibernate-Wake Architecture\n\n**Source:** [CF Long-Running Agents docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/concepts/long-running-agents/), [CF Worker limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/)\n\n**Critical constraint:** CF Workers/Queues/Crons are all hard-capped at **15 minutes** per invocation. A 1-hour loop cannot run in a single Worker invocation.\n\n**The correct CF pattern for 1 hour:**\n\nA **Durable Object** is the only CF primitive that supports true persistence with no compute cost when idle. The architecture:\n\n1. DO wakes via HTTP trigger or `schedule()` alarm.\n2. Drains one batch from queue (e.g., 5–10 items), persisting progress to SQLite after each item.\n3. Schedules next alarm for N seconds out (e.g., `scheduleEvery(30, \"processNextBatch\")`).\n4. Hibernates — zero cost until alarm fires.\n5. Repeats across the full 1-hour window via chained alarms.\n\n**For operations exceeding ~70–140 seconds:** Wrap in `keepAliveWhile()` to reset the inactivity eviction timer.\n\n**For metric reporting:** Persist a structured state object (step count, discoveries, errors, last-run timestamp) to SQLite — this doubles as recovery context and as the self-report payload.\n\n**Failure modes:**\n- In-memory variables do not survive hibernation — only `setState()` and `this.sql` persist. Forgetting this = silent state loss.\n- `keepAlive` works for minutes, not hours — use Workflows or callback patterns for single operations &gt;15 min.\n- Alarm at-least-once delivery: DO alarms can fire more than once under failure — operations must be idempotent.\n\n---\n\n## PATTERN 4 — Event-Driven Four-Pattern Matrix (Confluent)\n\n**Source:** [Confluent event-driven multi-agent systems](https://www.confluent.io/blog/event-driven-multi-agent-systems/)\n\nFour proven patterns for multi-agent coordination, each with a specific use case:\n\n| Pattern | Mechanism | Best For |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Orchestrator-Worker** | Central topic dispatch, consumer group balancing | Queue drain with load balancing |\n| **Hierarchical** | Recursive tree, each node is orchestrator for its subtree | Sibling competition inside a parent |\n| **Blackboard** | Shared topic as knowledge base, no direct agent comms | Async discovery logging |\n| **Market-Based** | Bid/ask topics, market-maker matching | Competing sibling agents — directly applicable |\n\n**For sibling competition:** The Market-Based pattern is the academic match. Agents post bids (discoveries/scores) to a bid topic; a market maker publishes rankings to an ask/result topic. No direct agent-to-agent coupling. Failure of one sibling does not block others.\n\n---\n\n## PATTERN 5 — MultiAgentBench KPI Framework (Academic Baseline)\n\n**Source:** [MultiAgentBench arxiv 2503.01935](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.01935v1)\n\nThe only peer-reviewed benchmark specifically for competitive multi-agent evaluation.\n\n**Metric collection approach:**\n- KPI = individual milestone contributions (nⱼ) / total milestones (M) — normalized 0–1.\n- An LLM-based detector continuously monitors the iterative process to identify which milestones have been achieved (not a human reviewer, not a regex — a judge LLM).\n- Communication Score (5-point scale), Planning Score (strategy adaptation), and Overall Coordination Score are averaged.\n\n**Time/iteration management:**\n- Max iterations vary by task (5 for research tasks, 20 for Minecraft).\n- Ablation result: **performance degrades beyond 7 iterations** — \"excessive iterations may lead to coordination degradation due to communication overhead.\"\n- Communication iteration limits are separately configured (default: 5).\n\n**Key finding for your use case:** More iterations ≠ better outcomes. There is an empirical degradation curve. For a 1-hour window, this implies bounded batch sizes with inter-batch pauses are better than a single continuous loop.\n\n---\n\n## PATTERN 6 — Temporal Workflow: Heartbeat-Based Deadline Enforcement\n\n**Source:** [Temporal queue draining post](https://martinuke0.github.io/posts/2026-03-24-orchestrating-distributed-task-queues-with-temporal-and-python-for-resilient-agentic-microservices/)\n\nTemporal is the most mature queue-drain-with-deadline framework. Key mechanics:\n\n- `start_to_close_timeout` on every activity — hard cap per operation (30s for payments, 10s for reservations in production examples).\n- **Heartbeat monitoring** for extended tasks: activities ping the Temporal server at intervals; if no heartbeat arrives within the window, the activity is assumed dead and retried.\n- Fan-out parallelism via child workflows for elastic backlog drain.\n- Monitored signals: `temporal_task_queue_pending_tasks` (backlog depth), `temporal_activity_failure_total`, `temporal_workflow_execution_latency`.\n- Alert threshold seen in production: `&gt;1000 tasks pending`.\n\n**Thundering herd mitigation:** Randomized backoff on retry storms — critical when a queue unfreezes after a blockage and all agents attempt simultaneous catch-up.\n\n---\n\n## SYNTHESIZED BEST PRACTICE FOR YOUR EXACT USE CASE\n\n**Profile:** 1-hour window, queue drain, discovery logging, self-report metrics, sibling competition.\n\n**Recommended architecture (composite of all above patterns):**\n\n### Execution model\nUse **Durable Objects + chained alarms** on CF, or **Temporal workflows** off-CF. Do NOT use a single long-running Worker/cron — both hit the 15-minute wall.\n\n### Loop structure\n```\ninit: { start_time, budget_seconds=3600, items_processed=0, discoveries=[], errors=[] }\n\non_each_alarm_wake:\n  1. Check: (now - start_time) &lt; budget_seconds → if no, write final report, stop\n  2. Pop N items from queue (N = 5–10 to stay under 15-min alarm window)\n  3. Process each item → classify result → append to discoveries[] if relevant\n  4. Persist state to SQLite / KV (idempotent write)\n  5. Schedule next alarm in 30–60 seconds\n  6. Write partial metrics to shared Blackboard topic / KV key\n```\n\n### Sibling competition\nUse the **Blackboard or Market-Based pattern**: each sibling writes its `{ agent_id, items_processed, discoveries_count, score }` to a shared KV key or topic on every alarm cycle. A lightweight scorer reads all entries and publishes a leaderboard. No direct sibling-to-sibling communication — decoupled by design.\n\n### Metric self-report\nPersist a structured object on every write cycle (not just at end):\n```json\n{ \"agent_id\": \"...\", \"run_start\": 1234567890, \"elapsed_s\": 1820,\n  \"items_processed\": 47, \"discoveries\": [...], \"errors\": 3,\n  \"last_checkpoint\": \"...\", \"score\": 0.74 }\n```\nThis is simultaneously the recovery checkpoint and the metrics payload — same write, dual purpose (CF Agents docs pattern).\n\n### Failure mode defenses\n| Risk | Mitigation |\n|---|---|\n| Silent state loss on eviction | Only write to `setState()` / SQLite, never in-memory |\n| Idempotency on alarm re-fire | Include `item_id` check before processing — skip if already in discoveries[] |\n| Context drift | Fresh context window per batch (Planner-Worker pattern) — do NOT carry full history across 60 iterations |\n| Coordination overhead | Cap inter-agent communication (MultiAgentBench finding: degrade &gt;7 coordination rounds) |\n| Queue exhaustion before deadline | Track `queue_depth` at each cycle; if 0, switch to discovery-consolidation mode rather than idling |\n| Thundering herd on restart | Randomized jitter on first alarm (Temporal pattern) |\n\n---\n\n## FAILURE MODES SUMMARY (PROVEN IN PRODUCTION)\n\n1. **Early termination** — models shortcut before window closes. Mitigation: Judge layer that explicitly checks \"has time budget expired?\" not just \"is task done?\"\n2. **Over-coordination** — quality-control integrator role becomes bottleneck. Mitigation: remove it; let Judge be the only evaluator.\n3. **Context drift** — long runs degrade goal fidelity. Mitigation: fresh context windows per batch.\n4. **In-memory state loss** — hibernation evicts non-persisted variables silently. Mitigation: SQLite-only state.\n5. **Coordination degradation** — multi-agent systems degrade beyond 7 coordination rounds (empirical). Mitigation: limit leaderboard sync frequency, not per-item.\n6. **Thundering herd** — all agents retry simultaneously after blockage. Mitigation: randomized jitter.\n7. **Duplicate processing** — alarm at-least-once delivery fires twice. Mitigation: idempotency check on item_id before every operation.\n\n---\n\nSources:\n- [Top 7 Agentic AI Frameworks in 2026](https://www.alphamatch.ai/blog/top-agentic-ai-frameworks-2026)\n- [AI Agent Compiling the research report.\n\n---\n\n# PCC-3 Research Report: Autonomous Agent Loop Patterns for Fixed Time Windows\n\n## WHAT WAS ASKED\n\nBest practices for running an AI agent autonomously for 1 hour that: drains a backlog queue, logs discoveries, self-reports metrics, and competes against sibling agents.\n\n---\n\n## PATTERN 1 — The Planner-Worker-Judge Triad (Most Proven)\n\n**Source:** [nibzard/awesome-agentic-patterns](https://github.com/nibzard/awesome-agentic-patterns/blob/main/patterns/planner-worker-separation-for-long-running-agents.md)\n\nThe single most battle-tested pattern for long-running autonomous work. Three roles:\n\n- **Planner** — explores the queue/codebase, spawns sub-planners, creates tasks. Planning itself is parallelized and recursive.\n- **Worker** — operates in isolation, no cross-worker coordination. Executes only its assigned task.\n- **Judge** — evaluates whether objective is met or iteration should continue.\n\n**Key mechanic:** \"Fresh starts\" at each cycle. Workers get a new context window per task to prevent drift and tunnel vision. This is the anti-pattern to long-context degradation.\n\n**Proven scale:** Hundreds of concurrent workers running for weeks on large codebases.\n\n**Failure modes (documented):**\n- Over-coordination: an \"integrator\" quality-control role created more bottlenecks than it solved — eliminated in production.\n- Early termination: models \"tend to stop early and take shortcuts\" — Judge layer is the mitigation.\n- Context drift: agents lose goal fidelity over long runs without fresh-start cycles.\n\n---\n\n## PATTERN 2 — LangGraph StateGraph with Hard Budget Caps\n\n**Source:** [MatterAI self-correcting loops guide](https://www.matterai.so/guides/agentic-workflows-building-self-correcting-loops-with-langgraph-and-crewai-state-machines), [LangGraph timeout docs](https://langchain-cn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/modules/agents/agent_executors/examples/max_time_limit.html)\n\nLangGraph implements time-bounded execution via `should_continue()` gates on conditional edges. The `AgentState` TypedDict tracks:\n\n- `iterations` — retry count hard cap (5–15 iterations recommended)\n- `total_tokens` — cumulative spend (50k token ceiling common)\n- `quality_score` — normalized LLM-as-judge score (0–1)\n- `errors` — classified failure modes (syntax / logic / timeout / API)\n\n**For a 1-hour time window:** LangGraph does NOT enforce wall-clock deadlines natively. You inject `start_time = time.time()` into the state at initialization, and `should_continue()` checks `time.time() - start_time &lt; 3600`. No built-in scheduler. Entirely custom.\n\n**Durable execution (LangGraph v1.0+):** Compile graph with PostgreSQL checkpointer — `StateSnapshot` saved at every super-step keyed by `thread_id`. If the runner dies mid-session, `resume_from_checkpoint(thread_id)` picks up exactly where it stopped. Validated in production.\n\n**Failure modes:**\n- No clock enforcement without custom implementation — easy to miss.\n- Checkpointer adds latency per step — 50–200ms per DB write at scale.\n- `max_iterations=15` without wall-clock guard allows runaway if LLM calls are fast.\n\n---\n\n## PATTERN 3 — Cloudflare Durable Objects: Hibernate-Wake Architecture\n\n**Source:** [CF Long-Running Agents docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/concepts/long-running-agents/), [CF Worker limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/)\n\n**Critical constraint:** CF Workers/Queues/Crons are all hard-capped at **15 minutes** per invocation. A 1-hour loop cannot run in a single Worker invocation.\n\n**The correct CF pattern for 1 hour:**\n\nA **Durable Object** is the only CF primitive that supports true persistence with no compute cost when idle. The architecture:\n\n1. DO wakes via HTTP trigger or `schedule()` alarm.\n2. Drains one batch from queue (e.g., 5–10 items), persisting progress to SQLite after each item.\n3. Schedules next alarm for N seconds out (e.g., `scheduleEvery(30, \"processNextBatch\")`).\n4. Hibernates — zero cost until alarm fires.\n5. Repeats across the full 1-hour window via chained alarms.\n\n**For operations exceeding ~70–140 seconds:** Wrap in `keepAliveWhile()` to reset the inactivity eviction timer.\n\n**For metric reporting:** Persist a structured state object (step count, discoveries, errors, last-run timestamp) to SQLite — this doubles as recovery context and as the self-report payload.\n\n**Failure modes:**\n- In-memory variables do not survive hibernation — only `setState()` and `this.sql` persist. Forgetting this = silent state loss.\n- `keepAlive` works for minutes, not hours — use Workflows or callback patterns for single operations &gt;15 min.\n- Alarm at-least-once delivery: DO alarms can fire more than once under failure — operations must be idempotent.\n\n---\n\n## PATTERN 4 — Event-Driven Four-Pattern Matrix (Confluent)\n\n**Source:** [Confluent event-driven multi-agent systems](https://www.confluent.io/blog/event-driven-multi-agent-systems/)\n\nFour proven patterns for multi-agent coordination, each with a specific use case:\n\n| Pattern | Mechanism | Best For |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Orchestrator-Worker** | Central topic dispatch, consumer group balancing | Queue drain with load balancing |\n| **Hierarchical** | Recursive tree, each node is orchestrator for its subtree | Sibling competition inside a parent |\n| **Blackboard** | Shared topic as knowledge base, no direct agent comms | Async discovery logging |\n| **Market-Based** | Bid/ask topics, market-maker matching | Competing sibling agents — directly applicable |\n\n**For sibling competition:** The Market-Based pattern is the academic match. Agents post bids (discoveries/scores) to a bid topic; a market maker publishes rankings to an ask/result topic. No direct agent-to-agent coupling. Failure of one sibling does not block others.\n\n---\n\n## PATTERN 5 — MultiAgentBench KPI Framework (Academic Baseline)\n\n**Source:** [MultiAgentBench arxiv 2503.01935](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.01935v1)\n\nThe only peer-reviewed benchmark specifically for competitive multi-agent evaluation.\n\n**Metric collection approach:**\n- KPI = individual milestone contributions (nⱼ) / total milestones (M) — normalized 0–1.\n- An LLM-based detector continuously monitors the iterative process to identify which milestones have been achieved (not a human reviewer, not a regex — a judge LLM).\n- Communication Score (5-point scale), Planning Score (strategy adaptation), and Overall Coordination Score are averaged.\n\n**Time/iteration management:**\n- Max iterations vary by task (5 for research tasks, 20 for Minecraft).\n- Ablation result: **performance degrades beyond 7 iterations** — \"excessive iterations may lead to coordination degradation due to communication overhead.\"\n- Communication iteration limits are separately configured (default: 5).\n\n**Key finding for your use case:** More iterations ≠ better outcomes. There is an empirical degradation curve. For a 1-hour window, this implies bounded batch sizes with inter-batch pauses are better than a single continuous loop.\n\n---\n\n## PATTERN 6 — Temporal Workflow: Heartbeat-Based Deadline Enforcement\n\n**Source:** [Temporal queue draining post](https://martinuke0.github.io/posts/2026-03-24-orchestrating-distributed-task-queues-with-temporal-and-python-for-resilient-agentic-microservices/)\n\nTemporal is the most mature queue-drain-with-deadline framework. Key mechanics:\n\n- `start_to_close_timeout` on every activity — hard cap per operation (30s for payments, 10s for reservations in production examples).\n- **Heartbeat monitoring** for extended tasks: activities ping the Temporal server at intervals; if no heartbeat arrives within the window, the activity is assumed dead and retried.\n- Fan-out parallelism via child workflows for elastic backlog drain.\n- Monitored signals: `temporal_task_queue_pending_tasks` (backlog depth), `temporal_activity_failure_total`, `temporal_workflow_execution_latency`.\n- Alert threshold seen in production: `&gt;1000 tasks pending`.\n\n**Thundering herd mitigation:** Randomized backoff on retry storms — critical when a queue unfreezes after a blockage and all agents attempt simultaneous catch-up.\n\n---\n\n## SYNTHESIZED BEST PRACTICE FOR YOUR EXACT USE CASE\n\n**Profile:** 1-hour window, queue drain, discovery logging, self-report metrics, sibling competition.\n\n**Recommended architecture (composite of all above patterns):**\n\n### Execution model\nUse **Durable Objects + chained alarms** on CF, or **Temporal workflows** off-CF. Do NOT use a single long-running Worker/cron — both hit the 15-minute wall.\n\n### Loop structure\n```\ninit: { start_time, budget_seconds=3600, items_processed=0, discoveries=[], errors=[] }\n\non_each_alarm_wake:\n  1. Check: (now - start_time) &lt; budget_seconds → if no, write final report, stop\n  2. Pop N items from queue (N = 5–10 to stay under 15-min alarm window)\n  3. Process each item → classify result → append to discoveries[] if relevant\n  4. Persist state to SQLite / KV (idempotent write)\n  5. Schedule next alarm in 30–60 seconds\n  6. Write partial metrics to shared Blackboard topic / KV key\n```\n\n### Sibling competition\nUse the **Blackboard or Market-Based pattern**: each sibling writes its `{ agent_id, items_processed, discoveries_count, score }` to a shared KV key or topic on every alarm cycle. A lightweight scorer reads all entries and publishes a leaderboard. No direct sibling-to-sibling communication — decoupled by design.\n\n### Metric self-report\nPersist a structured object on every write cycle (not just at end):\n```json\n{ \"agent_id\": \"...\", \"run_start\": 1234567890, \"elapsed_s\": 1820,\n  \"items_processed\": 47, \"discoveries\": [...], \"errors\": 3,\n  \"last_checkpoint\": \"...\", \"score\": 0.74 }\n```\nThis is simultaneously the recovery checkpoint and the metrics payload — same write, dual purpose (CF Agents docs pattern).\n\n### Failure mode defenses\n| Risk | Mitigation |\n|---|---|\n| Silent state loss on eviction | Only write to `setState()` / SQLite, never in-memory |\n| Idempotency on alarm re-fire | Include `item_id` check before processing — skip if already in discoveries[] |\n| Context drift | Fresh context window per batch (Planner-Worker pattern) — do NOT carry full history across 60 iterations |\n| Coordination overhead | Cap inter-agent communication (MultiAgentBench finding: degrade &gt;7 coordination rounds) |\n| Queue exhaustion before deadline | Track `queue_depth` at each cycle; if 0, switch to discovery-consolidation mode rather than idling |\n| Thundering herd on restart | Randomized jitter on first alarm (Temporal pattern) |\n\n---\n\n## FAILURE MODES SUMMARY (PROVEN IN PRODUCTION)\n\n1. **Early termination** — models shortcut before window closes. Mitigation: Judge layer that explicitly checks \"has time budget expired?\" not just \"is task done?\"\n2. **Over-coordination** — quality-control integrator role becomes bottleneck. Mitigation: remove it; let Judge be the only evaluator.\n3. **Context drift** — long runs degrade goal fidelity. Mitigation: fresh context windows per batch.\n4. **In-memory state loss** — hibernation evicts non-persisted variables silently. Mitigation: SQLite-only state.\n5. **Coordination degradation** — multi-agent systems degrade beyond 7 coordination rounds (empirical). Mitigation: limit leaderboard sync frequency, not per-item.\n6. **Thundering herd** — all agents retry simultaneously after blockage. Mitigation: randomized jitter.\n7. **Duplicate processing** — alarm at-least-once delivery fires twice. Mitigation: idempotency check on item_id before every operation.\n\n---\n\nSources:\n- [Top 7 Agentic AI Frameworks in 2026](https://www.alphamatch.ai/blog/top-agentic-ai-frameworks-2026)\n- [AI Agent
